FleetWise · UI/UX upgrade

Built so a farmer, a mechanic and a tractor driver all get it in one look.

Same green identity, same data, same backend calls — rebuilt around one rule: every screen answers “what do I do now?” before it shows a number. Mobile and desktop are designed separately, not stretched. Each screen below ships with the specific UX faults it fixes.

Every status now carries a shape + word + colour, so it survives sunlight, colour-blindness and a cracked screen.

Actions — icon + word, always
Destructive = two steps, always

“Delete Rooi Massey 385? This also hides 7 job cards and 31 readings.” Nothing is really deleted — the backend already soft-deletes — so the confirm says hides, and an undo toast follows.

Buttons are 48px, verbs not nouns, and never icon-only. Red is reserved for destroy — never for “overdue” buttons.

The audit · what was wrong
1

Seven counters before one instruction

The old page opened with Overdue / Due soon / Open faults / In workshop / spend / spend / Services OK. Oom Danie had to work out what to do. Now one ranked “Needs your attention” list tells him, with the button attached.

2

Every KPI tile linked to /reports

Tapping “2 Overdue” opened the reports page, not the two overdue machines. Fault rows linked to /faults — the list — never to the fault itself. Every row now deep-links to the thing it names.

3

Nine equal cards, nine scroll-screens

Spend trend, spend by type, cost per machine, fuel, expiries, nominations, faults, workshop, stale readings — all the same visual weight, all always open. Cut to four blocks; the breakdowns live in Costs & reports where someone actually wants them.

4

Empty states said “None”

Some cards used the nice EmptyState, others a bare grey “None”. Empty is the good outcome here — it now reads “Nothing needs you today” with a green tick, and the setup checklist takes the space.

5

The page was titled “Dashboard”

Jargon, and it told a multi-farm user nothing about which farm they were looking at. Replaced with a greeting, the farm name, the date and a one-line summary.

6

“Danie Kruger · owner” in 12px grey, at the bottom

Debug output shipped as UI, in the most-scrolled-to slot on the page. Removed — identity belongs in the shell, and it is there now.

7

14 nav items, 11 of them hidden in “More”

The daily action — report a problem — was nowhere in the chrome. Mobile now has 4 tabs plus a permanent green Report button; the sidebar drops to three short groups with the long tail behind “Everything else”.

8

Machines were names, not machines

The photo column existed but the dashboard never used it. A driver recognises the green John Deere long before he reads “JD 6120, serial L06120…”. Photo first, name right next to it — never instead of it.

Backend untouched

Same queries, same entitlement gate, same multi-site scoping, same retired/sold exclusions. Every number on this screen already exists in the dashboard query — I only changed which ones get to be loud, and what you can tap.

The audit · what was wrong
1

Every status was the same grey

The list rendered <Badge tone="neutral"> for all six statuses — Working, In workshop, Standby, Out of service, Retired, Sold looked identical. A broken machine and a working one were visually the same row. Now status is a coloured dot + word, and “Workshop · 12 d” carries its own age.

2

A filter form you had to submit

Five dropdowns and a “Search” button in a card ate the first ~180px — the entire first screen on a phone — and nothing happened until you pressed submit. Replaced with filter chips that apply on tap, plus three one-tap presets (All / Needs work / Tractors).

3

Raw meter values

The row printed {current_reading} {meter_type} straight from the database: “184320 km”, “6412 hours”. No thousands separator, database column name as the unit. Now 184,320 km with when it was last read underneath — because a stale reading is the thing that breaks service dates.

4

The photo was 36 pixels

The schema does real work for this — primary_attachment_id, batch-signed URLs — and it was spent on a 36px thumbnail. Mobile now leads with a 132px photo (the way a driver identifies a machine), desktop keeps a 46px thumb because a table is for scanning columns.

5

“—” in pale grey for no service plan

A machine with no service plan showed a sand-300 dash — invisible, and hiding a real to-do. It is now a tappable “Set up a plan” chip, which is also how the farm hits the 80%-of-machines adoption target.

6

No count, no result feedback

Nothing on the page said how many machines there were, or that a filter was hiding some. Now: “12 on the farm · 2 need service · 1 in the workshop” in the header and “Showing 11 of 12” by the filters.

7

One empty state for two different problems

“No machines” showed the same copy whether the farm had none or the filter matched none — and offered “Add machine” when the fix was clearing a filter. Split: a warm first-run screen with a ghost preview of the filled list, versus a “nothing matches — clear the filter” state.

8

A desktop table with nothing to do

Seven read-only columns and no row action: to log an hour reading you opened the machine, logged it, came back, lost your place. Rows now carry a “log hours” button and a ⋯ menu; selection enables bulk status change, template apply and QR printing — the things onboarding actually needs.

Backend untouched

Same machines query, same searchParam filters (type · status · q · cc · dept · sort · dir · retired), same signed-photo batching, same RLS/farm scoping. Cost-per-hour comes from the cost ledger that already feeds the reports. The chips write the same URL params the form did.

The audit · what was wrong
1

Eight identical grey boxes, four of them jargon

Status, Date in, Date out, Meter reading, Reported problem, Diagnosis, Work performed, Recommendations — all rows={2}, all equal weight, on a phone in a workshop. Now three plain questions: What was wrong? What did you find? What did you do? — and on mobile, one per step.

2

Two submit buttons, and the wrong one was primary

The line form’s Add was variant="primary" while the job card’s own Save was variant="secondary" — so the loudest button on the page saved a spare part, not the job. The Save button is gone entirely: it already autosaves, so the footer now holds the only real decision — is this job done?

3

It autosaved every 500ms and never said so

Good engineering, invisible to the user — while a Save button sat there implying the opposite. A quiet “Saved a moment ago” now sits in the header, which is what makes it safe to walk away mid-job.

4

You could only discover the blocker by being blocked

“Mark completed” opened a modal, then disabled its own confirm button with disabled={noMeter} and a red line of text. The requirement is now visible in the footer before you try, with the field right there to fill in.

5

Status was a dropdown of database values

Five states hidden in a <Select> — you had to open it to learn where the job stood. Now a visible pipeline: Reported → Taken on → Busy with it → Waiting for parts → Done. Same five values, same server action.

6

VAT explained in arrow notation

The live preview read R968.30 incl → R842.00 ex + R126.30 vat. Now the incl-VAT toggle is a 48px row that says it in words: “So R842.00 for the part, R126.30 VAT.” The 16px checkbox became the whole row.

7

No running total while you worked

Lines were added one by one with no sense of the job’s cost until the list page. The total now sits above the lines and moves as you add — the number the owner will ask about.

8

The recovered-draft banner looked like an error

Amber warning styling, with Restore / Discard as 12px buttons at py-1 — roughly 24px tall, on a phone, for the one moment the app is saving your bacon. Recovery is now silent and automatic; the header just confirms it saved.

Backend untouched

Same saveJobCard, addLine, completeJobCard and approveJobCard server actions with the same field names; same localStorage draft key; same offline queueing with idempotency UUIDs; same VAT maths from exVatCents; the DB trigger still owns the canonical total. The completion confirm dialog stays — it just no longer hides the reason you can’t confirm.

The audit · what was wrong
1

Twenty cards, one scroll, no hierarchy

1,400 lines rendering meter history, fuel, service plan, service kit, compliance, budget, timeline, who operated, lifetime stats, utilisation, finance, watch items, job cards, checklists, outside work and attachments — every one an open <Card> of equal weight. Now five tabs, and Overview holds only what changes a decision today.

2

Delete had no confirm at all

You asked for this one. The soft-delete fired straight from the button. It now costs one deliberate step that names what else disappears — 7 job cards, 31 readings, R184,200 of history — and warns that job card #1042 is still open. Same deleted_at soft delete underneath, so “hides” is the honest word.

3

The graph vanished when you needed it most

MeterGraph does if (pts.length < 2) return null — so a machine with one reading showed an empty card with a title and nothing else. Exactly the machine whose readings you need to chase. Now that state says so, and asks for a reading.

4

Graph axis labels at 12px in sand-400

The figcaption printed 2026-02-14 · 6100 hours in text-xs text-sand-400 — about 2:1 contrast, in a tractor cab in the sun. Values now sit above each bar at readable weight, with the month underneath.

5

The red alert card was one of twenty

A machine standing broken got <Card className="border-status-overdue bg-red-50"> — the right instinct, but placed in a stack where it scrolled away. It is now pinned at the top of Overview with the job card link on it, and the phone shows it under the photo.

6

Jargon headings straight from the spec

“Utilisation”, “Lifetime stats”, “Compliance”, “Watch items”, “Service kit”, “Meter history”. Now: Hours it has worked, Keep an eye on, Papers & licence, What happened to it, What it costs.

7

The machine’s photo wasn’t the hero on a phone

On the one screen where you are standing next to the machine, the photo was a small thumbnail among cards. Mobile now opens with a 216px photo, the status over it, and the three things a driver does — log hours, add diesel, job card.

8

Success was a query string

Every action redirected to ?saved=reading, ?saved=watch, ?error=Enter+a+valid+reading — server-worded errors in the URL bar. Same redirects, but the flash is now a plain sentence at the top of the screen, and the reading form validates before it posts.

Backend untouched

All twenty sections still exist and still read the same queries — they are grouped, not removed. Same addReading (with its usage-log write and newest-reading guard), setWatchStatus, service, kit, licence, budget and QR actions; same role gates; same PDF routes for the warranty and sale packs. Tabs are client-side only.

No login, no training, no help desk — a driver holds a cracked phone next to a broken tractor, in the sun, maybe in Afrikaans, maybe not confident reading either language. The old page opened with four stacked forms and no labels. Everything below is designed for that moment.

The audit · what was wrong
1

Four open forms, on the no-training screen

Report a problem, log a reading, log a service and log fuel — all expanded at once. Someone who scanned to report smoke had to scroll past three other forms. Now one question, four big tiles, and only the chosen form opens.

2

Every field was placeholder-only — no labels at all

Ten inputs on the public page, not one <label> between them: the question disappears the moment you start typing. For a nervous first-time user that is the worst possible pattern. Every field now has a real label that stays put.

3

It never showed you which machine you scanned

Just the name as text — no photo, no confirmation. Stickers get swapped between machines and QR codes get scanned from the wrong side of a shed. The page now leads with the photo and “This is the machine you scanned”, so a wrong report is caught in one second.

4

Five ghost buttons and a dropdown, all the same weight

Each fault offered Acknowledge, Start work, To job card, an assignee <Select> + Assign, and Resolve — every one variant="ghost" size="sm". When everything is quiet, nothing is obvious. Now one green action per row (Make a job card) and the rest sit back.

5

Sorted alphabetically by status, not by how bad it is

The query was .order("status") — so “acknowledged” came before “open” because of the alphabet, and a machine standing dead could sit under a torn seat. Same query, urgency first: stopped, then limping, then FYI.

6

The photo of the broken part was 64 pixels

A driver’s photo is the single most useful thing in a fault report, and it rendered at h-16 w-16. The urgent fault now shows it at 132px, and the voice note is a labelled play button with its length — not a bare <audio controls>.

7

Emoji doing the work of icons

The public page used a tractor emoji as the logo, a fuel-pump emoji in a heading and a pin emoji for the map link — rendering differently on every Android in the district, and read aloud as “tractor” by screen readers. Replaced with the app’s own icon set.

8

“No faults” looked the same as a broken page

An empty fault list is the best news on the farm, and it got the generic EmptyState. Now it celebrates — “Nothing broken today”, with the last thing that got fixed, and a way to report something if you did find a problem.

Backend untouched

The public page still runs token-gated through the service client with zero anon DB access, still posts to /api/public/fault, still uses OfflineForm queueing and the same submitReading / submitService / submitFuel actions — including the plan gate that hides diesel on farms without it. Faults keep acknowledgeFault, startFault, assignFault, resolveFault and createJobCard with the same hidden fields and role checks; photos and voice notes still come from signed storage URLs.
S06

Contractor — the workshop’s own portal

replaces /contractor and /work/[id]

A contractor is a business, not a farm worker. They serve many farms, they get paid, and their day is a queue: what came in, what’s on the bench, what I can invoice. The old portal grouped work by the eight database lifecycle values instead — so “what must I do now” was never on screen.

The audit · what was wrong
1

The eight-step stepper, as tiny scrolling pills

Requested › viewed › quoted › accepted › in progress › completed › invoiced › closed — eight text-xs chips in an overflow-x-auto row, so on a phone you saw three and had to swipe. Now a real progress line with plain names — They asked → You saw it → Price sent → They said yes → Busy with it → Done → Paid up.

2

Two competing ways to change status

Contextual quick buttons and a dropdown listing all eight values — including ones that move the job backwards — sitting right next to each other. Now one obvious Next step button in the footer; the unusual moves (hold, decline) sit apart on the right.

3

Money entered in a 112px box labelled “R”

Quote and invoice both used a bare <input className="w-28"> with placeholder-only labelling and a 16px VAT checkbox — for the number this whole business runs on. Now labelled fields at 48px, and the VAT toggle is a full row that explains itself.

4

Work grouped by database lifecycle value

Eight possible groups on one page, in enum order, each a badge and a count. A contractor’s actual question is “what must I do today”. Regrouped into four: New · Waiting on the farmer · On my bench · Ready to invoice — same statuses underneath.

5

R14,200 — but is that a quote or a bill?

The amount rendered with the word “quote” or “invoice” after it in text-xs text-sand-400 — the faintest text on the card carried the meaning of the biggest number. The label now sits above the amount at readable weight.

6

Another submit-to-filter form

Kind chips applied instantly, but status, client and sort sat in three <Select>s behind a Search button — two interaction models on one card. The queue now needs no filtering to be useful; farm and search are one row at the top.

7

Raw ISO dates everywhere

updated_at.slice(0, 10) printed 2026-07-28 on every card and every timeline row. What a contractor needs is “2 days ago” — how long the farmer has been waiting.

8

The Pro upsell was a dashed grey box

Locked analytics showed a dashed placeholder, a lock line and “contact Rapid Rise” as 12px grey text with a chevron — no price, no way to act. It now names the benefit in the contractor’s words and has a real button. The gate itself is unchanged.

Backend untouched

Same workshop-scoped query with the belt-and-braces workshop_id filter on top of RLS, so a contractor still never sees another workshop’s work on a shared farm. Same updateWorkRequestStatus, addWorkRequestNote, setWorkRequestQuote, setWorkRequestInvoice and convertToJobCard actions; all eight statuses still exist and every transition is still reachable; the client_analytics plan gate and the kind-based focus defaults are unchanged.

The audit · what was wrong
1

Two forms, fourteen inputs, side by side

“Log draw” (machine, tank, litres, meter, cost, date, driver, activity) and “Log fill” (tank, date, litres, cost, supplier, invoice no.) both open at once. On a phone at the pump that is a wall of boxes. Split: filling a machine is a 3-step wizard; a tanker delivery is its own screen for whoever does the paperwork.

2

Four words for two ideas

The KPI row read Purchased · Delivered · Attributed · Issued — bookkeeping words for “diesel that came in” and “diesel that went into machines”. Now it’s one line in the header: 4,180 ℓ came in · 3,940 ℓ went into machines.

3

The tank balance was the last line on the page

Reconciliation — the number that catches diesel theft — sat under both forms as a small text row. It is now the first thing you see, drawn as a tank, with the shortfall called out in rands: “Kamp 4 is 180 ℓ short — that’s R4,100.”

4

A whole anomaly engine, shown as a hover tooltip

Migration 0242 computes consumption anomalies properly, and the UI rendered 16 bars min-w-[3px] wide whose only explanation was a title attribute — invisible on touch. The finding is now a sentence: normal 0.63 ℓ/h, now 1.04 ℓ/h, with a job-card button.

5

Eight report cards, all open, all equal

Cost per machine, spend by type, compliance, recurring problems, fuel, budget, utilisation, contractors — one long scroll of same-sized cards. Reports answer a question; they are now six tabs, and the landing tab leads with the one finding worth acting on.

6

Nine separate CSV links, scattered

cost · by-type · compliance · problems · fuel · budgets · utilisation · contractors · workbook.xlsx, each a small link on its own card, plus an audit-pack PDF at the top. Now one Download everything button, and each table keeps a quiet “this table” export. Same routes.

7

“R126 per hour” with nothing to compare it to

Cost per machine was a plain sorted list. A number only means something next to another number — every row now carries a bar and a plain verdict (3× avg / Normal), so the outlier finds you.

8

The rebate was never mentioned

The activity dropdown exists precisely so a farm can claim the SARS diesel refund — and nothing on the page said so, which is why drivers left it blank. It now asks “What was it doing?” with the claimable ones marked, and the split feeds a logbook button.

Backend untouched

Same addFuelIssue and addFuelDelivery actions with the same field names, the same nine FUEL_ACTIVITIES values, the same tank-balance maths and the same brim-to-brim computeConsumption — the wizard just posts the same form in three steps. Reports still read reports/data.ts unchanged; all nine CSV routes, the workbook and the audit-pack PDF keep their URLs.

The audit · what was wrong
1

Permanent erasure as a small grey link

erasePerson anonymises a human being across the whole database and bans their login for a hundred years. It sat in a row of variant="ghost" size="sm" buttons next to Export, behind a browser confirm(). Now: hidden behind ⋯, a sheet that lists exactly what happens, type-the-name to unlock, and a pointer to the reversible option.

2

VAT entered in basis points

The field was vat_rate_bps with a default of 1500. A farmer reads that as fifteen hundred percent, or types 15 and silently sets VAT to 0.15%. Now it reads 15 % and the page converts — the column still stores basis points.

3

Seventeen numbers, no idea what any of them do

Eight cards of bare number inputs — due-soon hours, stale days, anomaly %, repair-replace %, utilisation hours per day, AARTO lead days — with a label and nothing else. Every setting now says what it changes on this farm: “that means the Massey goes amber at 1,225 hours”.

4

Roles printed straight from the database

<Badge className="capitalize">{u.role}</Badge> rendered “Operator”, “Workshop”, “Rr_admin”. And nothing anywhere explained the difference between a mechanic and an operator — the choice you make when inviting someone. Each row now names the job and what it may do, with a reference panel beside it.

5

“Active: No” in danger red

A person who left the farm is not an error, but the table gave them a red No badge — the same red as an overdue service. Replaced with plain states: signing in today / invited but never signed in / no login needed / turned off.

6

Sorted alphabetically by role enum

.order("role") put manager, mechanic and operator above owner, because m comes before o. The list now runs by seniority, with you at the top and people who have left at the bottom.

7

One Save button, eight cards down

Change the first field, then scroll past seven more cards to save — and no indication anything was unsaved on the way. Settings now save as you change them, with a quiet confirmation in the header, and the eight cards became seven named groups you can jump between.

8

Two big switches as 20px checkboxes

“Approval required” changes how every job card on the farm behaves, and “cost visible to operators” decides who sees money — both were h-5 w-5 checkboxes with a one-line label. Now full-width switches that spell out the consequence of each position.

Backend untouched

Same inviteUser, setUserActive and erasePerson actions — including the guarded erase_personal_data RPC, the auth scrub and the self-erase block. Same invite permission rules (a farm boss may still only invite manager / mechanic / operator to their own farm). Every settings key writes the same JSON column with the same names and units — vat_rate_bps still receives 1500; only the label and the ×100 happen in the browser. The team CSV export keeps its route.

The audit · what was wrong
1

Two email boxes on one small screen

A password form and a magic-link form, each with its own name="email" field, separated by an “OR”. Autofill fills the first, the user taps the second button, nothing happens. Now one email box, magic link as the main path, password behind a second button.

2

A bilingual app with an English-only front door

Every t() call on the login page is made without a locale — language lives on the profile, which nobody has loaded yet. So an Afrikaans farm’s first screen is English, with no way to change it. The toggle now sits on the login page and is remembered on the device.

3

A setup step that ticks itself

In onboarding/page.tsx, step 1 and step 3 share done: machines > 0. Add one machine and two steps go green — including “put QR stickers on”, which nobody has done. That is why farms reach the dashboard with no stickers printed, and the whole no-login flow never starts.

4

Raw Supabase errors, in the URL bar

redirect(`/login?error=${error.message}`) puts “Invalid login credentials” or “Email rate limit exceeded” on screen and in the address bar — first contact with the product, in developer English.

5

“Check your email” was a green strip above the same form

?sent=1 showed a small Flash and left both forms sitting there, so people typed their address again. It is now its own screen: which address, what to do if it hasn’t arrived, a countdown before resending, and a way to fix a typo.

6

Nothing for the people with no email

Much of the workforce this is built for has no work email — they use the QR stickers, which need no login at all. The login screen never said so, so drivers got stuck at the door.

7

Placeholder-only fields, again

Both email boxes and the password box were labelled by placeholder only — on the most anxious screen in the product, the question vanishes the moment you type.

8

Finished steps kept shouting

A completed step stayed full size at opacity-80 with its button still there, so the one thing left to do had no more presence than the three already done. Done steps now collapse to a line and only the next action is loud.

Backend untouched

Same signInWithPassword and signInWithOtp calls, same /auth/callback?next=/dashboard redirect, same requireProfile gate. Errors still round-trip through the query string — the page just translates known codes into sentences. Onboarding reads the same three counts; step 3 needs its own condition (QR labels printed) instead of reusing the machine count.

The audit · what was wrong
1

“Act into farm” doesn’t act into anything

impersonateFarm calls log_admin_farm_access and redirects with ?entered=1. No farm context is set, no session changes. The flash reads “Support access logged” — staff reasonably believe they are inside. There is no banner and no exit because there is no mode. This design gives the mode a persistent amber bar and one Leave this farm button.

2

Entering a customer’s farm was a small secondary button

Reading a farmer’s private data sat as variant="secondary" size="sm" in a card header, with no confirmation and no reason captured. It now asks why first — the reason goes into the log the farm can read.

3

The churn radar was the last column

Scope calls this table a churn radar, and “last activity” was the rightmost column, red only after 14 days, sorted by signup date instead. Now: quiet farms first, four counters above the table, and the row action is Call them.

4

A create form permanently occupying the top of the page

“Create farm” is done a few times a month; it sat above the list every single visit, pushing 31 farms down the page. It is now a New farm button.

5

Money shown three ways, hedged in 12px grey

Per-vehicle, indicative subtotal and “(incl. VAT · 12 × R149.50)” in a <dl>, with the crucial caveat — no charge is made — as the smallest text on the card. The caveat is now a visible amber note beside the numbers.

6

Two forms and a Save button per farm

Plan, billing period and status each needed a dropdown plus a shared Save — three fields and a submit for what is usually one change. Autosave, same server action, same three values.

7

The access log said “admin · impersonate”

Enum values and toLocaleString timestamps, with “admin” as the fallback name. For a log a customer may one day demand to see, it now reads “Nadia went in — 12 minutes · fixed a duplicated machine”.

8

Nothing marked this as the internal tool

The console used the same green farmer chrome, distinguished only by a 12px grey “Rapid Rise admin” label — so a screen-share couldn’t tell staff view from customer view. It is now dark and badged STAFF ONLY, which also makes the amber impersonation bar unmistakable.

Backend untouched

Same requireRole(["rr_admin"]) gate on the layout and both pages, same createFarm / updateFarm actions and RLS insert policy, same log_admin_farm_access RPC from migration 0206, same perVehicleMonthlyCents and subscriptionSubtotalCents from entitlements, and the same reuse of inviteUser / setUserActive with the back param. The console stays English-only.

One backend change needed here

The amber bar can only exist if impersonation has state. That needs a farm-context cookie set on enter and cleared on leave — plus a second log_admin_farm_access(…, 'exit') call so the log shows duration.

This is the one place I can’t deliver the UX without touching behaviour, so it is flagged rather than assumed. The alternative — leave the button as a pure log entry — means renaming it to “Log that I looked”, which is honest but not what Scope §4.9 asks for.
S11

The driver’s own home

new · the operator role currently lands on /dashboard

The least computer-literate role has no screen of its own. requireRole sends every denied user to /dashboard?error=forbidden — so a driver who taps the wrong tab lands on the owner’s money dashboard, and error=forbidden is never rendered as anything a person can read. Meanwhile the QR flow (S05) proves the right shape for this user: one big thing per screen, photos, no jargon. This gives the signed-in driver the same treatment.

The audit · what was wrong
1

Denied users are dumped on the owner’s dashboard

requireRole ends with redirect("/dashboard?error=forbidden") for every role. A driver who taps the wrong tab lands on a page of Rands and cost charts — the one thing the farm can switch off for operators. Send them to their own home instead.

2

“forbidden” is never rendered

The redirect appends ?error=forbidden and the dashboard has no Flash for it — so the screen simply changes with no explanation. Either say “that part is for the boss” in plain words, or don’t show the door at all. This design does the latter.

3

The hardest user got the generic shell

An operator sees the same sidebar, the same bottom tabs and the same “More” sheet as the owner — a navigation system built for someone with fourteen destinations, handed to someone with four tasks. Their home is now four full-width tiles at 20px, and nothing else.

4

No way to pick a machine without reading

Every machine chooser in the app is a <Select> of names and serials. For a driver, a two-column grid of photographs — most-used first — is faster and needs no literacy at all.

5

Nothing told them their report landed

A driver reports a fault and never hears anything again, so next time he tells the foreman instead and the system goes quiet. Their home now closes the loop: “Everything you reported has been seen — Piet is working on the green John Deere.”

6

Their language setting was never used on their screens

Invites default language to af, which is the right instinct — but the driver’s journey (login, QR landing) is exactly where t() gets called without a locale. Shown here in Afrikaans, as the data says it should be.

7

Scan was buried, though it’s the whole point

QR is how this role is meant to work, and there was no scan entry in the signed-in app at all — only the sticker itself. It is now the first and loudest tile.

8

Sign out hidden in a sheet behind “More”

On a shared bakkie phone, signing out matters more than for anyone else — and it sat two taps deep inside the overflow menu. It’s now a plain button at the bottom of their home.

Backend untouched

No new tables, actions or policies. This is the existing operator role, the existing fault / reading / fuel actions (the same ones the QR pages already post to), and the same cost visible to operators setting deciding that no money appears. The only change is where an operator lands — a role branch on the post-login redirect and on requireRole’s fallback, both one line.
S12

Owner inbox — money waiting on you

replaces /inbox

Fifth defect. acceptQuote and approveInvoice commit the farm to real money — and both fire from a size="sm" button with no confirmation step at all. A mis-tap on a phone approves a R14,200 invoice. Meanwhile the machine name beside it is a link, so the two tap targets sit millimetres apart.

The audit · what was wrong
1

Approving money had no confirmation

acceptQuote and approveInvoice commit the farm to thousands of rands, and both fired straight from a size="sm" button. Now a sheet that names the amount, shows quote against bill, and says what the approval tells the contractor.

2

The approve button sat beside a link, on a phone

The row put the machine-name link, three icon-only contact buttons and the approve submit in one flex row — five targets in a few millimetres, the largest of which spends money. Now one card per decision, one primary button.

3

You could only say yes

Accept and Approve were the only actions on the card. Declining a price, or querying a bill that doesn’t match its quote, had no path at all — so those conversations happen on WhatsApp and the system loses them. Both now have a visible button.

4

Four counters splitting two facts

Outstanding quotes · quote value · outstanding invoices · invoice value — count and money as separate tiles, so the owner had to pair them mentally. Replaced with one total and a two-line split, plus what it does to the month.

5

A bill for finished work looked like a quote

Both rendered the same way, distinguished by a workStatusLabel badge and the button’s wording. One is “may they start”, the other is “the work is done, pay them” — different decisions, now visibly different cards.

6

Contact was three unlabelled icons

Phone, WhatsApp and mail as ghost size="sm" glyphs with only an aria-label — invisible to the low-literacy users the app is built for, and below tap-target size.

7

Active work nested three levels deep

Grouped by machine, each group a heading plus an indented list of kind · title · contractor · priority · amount · status — six pieces of metadata per line at 12–14px. Flattened to one row per job with the photo doing the identifying.

8

Read state needed a button press per item

Every notification carried its own 20px-tall “read” form, and the date rendered toLocaleDateString("en-ZA"). Now opening the thing marks it read, and dates are relative.

Backend untouched

Same requireRole(["owner","manager"]) gate, same acceptQuote / approveInvoice / markInboxRead / markAllInboxRead actions, same INBOX_ACTION_STATUSES set deciding what needs a decision, same notification templates through formatNotification and notificationUrl, same deliver_after filtering and 40-row limit, same contact.ts helpers for tel / WhatsApp / mail. The confirmation step is a client-side dialog in front of the existing submit; “decline” and “query” post the existing updateWorkRequestStatus transitions that already exist for the contractor side.

And the feature built to prevent it — auto-suggesting who was driving from the usage logs — was collapsed inside a <details> behind a 12px disclosure link.

The audit · what was wrong
1

A legal deadline in 12px grey

The nomination deadline decides whether the fine lands on the farm or the driver, and it rendered as a raw ISO date in text-xs text-sand-500, third line down. It is now a countdown block — 4 days left — and the card border turns red.

2

The clever part was hidden in a <details>

Naming the driver — the entire point of the screen, backed by a real usage-log lookup — sat behind a summary styled text-xs font-medium, which then revealed a select plus a text input plus a save button. Now the suggestion is the card, with one confirm button.

3

Deleting a fine was a 12px red text link

deleteFine fired from text-xs text-status-overdue with px-1 padding and no confirmation — on a record with a legal deadline attached.

4

Twelve fields to log one fine

And a separate GET form before it, so you filled in a vehicle and date, pressed “Find driver”, and only then met the real form. Now: the notice arrives, you pick the vehicle and the date, and everything else can be filled in later or not at all.

5

The suggestion never said why

“Suggested: Thabo Mokoena” in a brand-50 strip. The evidence — he logged diesel into that bakkie that day, at that reading — was fetched and thrown away. Showing it is what makes the owner trust the guess enough to act on it.

6

A status dropdown and a Set button on every card

Five statuses in a select, then a secondary submit, repeated per fine — two interactions to record “the driver paid it”. The states are now plain rows, and the common transitions are buttons.

7

Three ISO dates per fine

Offence date, fine date and deadline all printed as 2026-07-21, tabular-nums, in a run of dot-separated fragments. Now “Tuesday 21 July”, and the deadline is a countdown.

8

“No pending” with no explanation

A bare EmptyState with a title and nothing else, on the screen where empty means you are legally in the clear. And no per-driver pattern anywhere, though the data supports it — repeat offenders are exactly what an owner wants to see.

Backend untouched

Same checkEntitlement("aarto") server-side gate — under-plan farms still never fetch fine data. Same createFine / identifyDriver / updateFineStatus / deleteFine actions and the same FINE_STATUSES list. The driver suggestion is the existing usage_logs query on machine_id + occurred_on — I only render the evidence it already returns. Deadline urgency still comes from nominationDeadlineStatus() with the farm’s aarto_nomination_lead_days. Owner/manager-only management is unchanged.

The audit · what was wrong
1

You cannot actually do a check

The page lists template definitions with Edit, Duplicate and Delete. There is no “start a check”, no history of checks done, and nothing linking a template to a machine. The admin screen exists; the daily habit it is meant to support does not.

2

A chevron that does nothing

When the user can’t edit a row, the actions are replaced by <span><ChevronRightIcon /></span> — a right-arrow that is not a link and goes nowhere. It reads as “tap for more” to every user who sees it.

3

Delete a template with one click, no confirm

A bare <button> in red text beside Edit and Duplicate, firing deleteChecklistTemplate immediately.

4

“Global” and “Farm” as badges

Multi-tenancy vocabulary on a farmer’s screen. It means “Rapid Rise wrote this one” versus “you wrote this one” — say that, or don’t say it at all.

5

“6 fields · updated 2026-07-14”

Field count is a schema fact, not a reason to use something. What matters is who did it last and what it found — both available and neither shown.

6

Edit, Duplicate and Delete at equal weight

Three actions on every row, one of them destructive, none of them the thing anyone came to do.

7

The driver can’t reach it

Operators are excluded from canManageFarm, which is right for editing templates — but they are the people who should be doing the checks, and there is no operator-facing route at all. It now hangs off the QR scan and the driver’s home.

8

Nothing said what a check is for

A driver won’t report a worn belt if he thinks it lands him in trouble. The check screen now says plainly that nothing here goes on a bill — it goes to Piet.

Backend untouched

Same checklist_templates and checklist_template_fields tables with the same soft-delete filters, the same global-vs-farm RLS split, and the same duplicateChecklistTemplate / deleteChecklistTemplate actions. Template editing stays owner/manager/mechanic; RR admin still owns the global rows. The run-a-check screens write checklist responses through the existing fault/attachment paths — no new tables.

Settings above the content

Quiet hours as two 0–23 number boxes

type="number" min={0} max={23} labelled “Start” and “End”, with placeholder “inherit”. A farmer must work out that 20 means eight at night, and “inherit” is a programming word. Now a time picker that states the result in words.

Every row is a <Card> with text and a “read” button — no link to the thing it is about, even though notificationUrl() exists and the inbox uses it. You are told a machine broke and cannot get to it.

A 20px-tall “read” button per row

px-2 py-0.5 text-xs — roughly 20px high, on the row you are already touching. Opening the notification should mark it read; the button disappears.

5

Read state as opacity-75

Fading the whole card dims the text to roughly 3:1 contrast — below the accessible minimum, in bright sun, on a phone. Read items now use full-contrast secondary text and simply lose the dot.

6

Sixty rows, no grouping, no icons

A flat list of up to 60 identical cards. A breakdown and “hours are stale” look the same. Now grouped into New / Earlier, with the alert type carrying a coloured icon.

7

Dates as toLocaleDateString("en-ZA")

Every row stamped 2026/07/28 in text-xs text-sand-400 — the palest text in the design system, carrying the only ordering cue. Now “2 days ago”.

8

“Mark all read” as a ghost button

The one bulk action on the page, styled to disappear — and it only renders when something is unread, so the control moves around between visits.

Backend untouched

Same notifications query with the same deliver_after filter and 60-row limit, same formatNotification templates with machine-name resolution, same markRead / markAllRead / setNotificationPrefs actions writing the same four user columns, same PushToggle component and service-worker subscription. 1

A login credential printed on the page

A freshly-minted contractor login URL renders in a card at the top as copyable plain text, with no warning about what it is. Disclosures inside disclosures

Delete as 12px red text, no confirm — twice

“Connected” / “Not connected” as badges

Two words that decide whether a workshop can quote you inside FleetWise or must phone. Neither says what it means. Now spelled out: “Sends quotes through FleetWise”.

5

“Suggested” never says by whom or why

A curated global list appears under a one-word heading. Is it advertising? Vetted? Nearby? Now: “Rapid Rise knows these workshops in your district”, with distance.

6

“No contact details” in the palest grey

A partner with no phone number is useless — that is a to-do, not a footnote in text-xs text-sand-400. It now carries an amber row and a button to fix it.

7

Contact buttons that appear and vanish

Call, WhatsApp and Email each render only if that field is filled, so the row of buttons is a different width and order on every card. Nothing sits in a predictable place.

8

Nothing said who you actually use

An alphabetical contact list, when the cost ledger already knows this farm spent R31,200 with Botha Diesel and R6,400 with Kareekloof. Spend per partner now sits beside the list.

Backend untouched

Same partners query and farm-vs-global split, same seven KINDS, same createPartner / updatePartner / deletePartner / adoptSuggested / inviteContractor / sendLoginUrl actions, and the same telHref / waHref / mailtoHref helpers with their prefill strings. Owner/manager manage farm rows, RR admin owns the global ones, RLS unchanged. The login URL is still generated the same way — it is handed straight to the WhatsApp or mail intent instead of being rendered.

1

Six statuses, three colours

statusTone gives completed and approved green, waiting_parts amber, and reported / open / in_progress all the same blue. The three states a mechanic moves between daily are visually identical. Each state now has its own colour and plain wording.

2

Creating a job card is a dropdown and an instant commit

Pick a machine from a select in the page header, press New, and a job card exists — with <input type="hidden" name="type" value="repair">. Every job is a “repair” whether it is a service, an inspection or a rebuild, and mis-selecting the machine creates a real record you must then delete.

You can’t see whose job it is

The query selects id, type, status, date_in, total_cents, machine_id — no assignee, no contractor. On a farm with a mechanic and two outside workshops, the list cannot answer “what is mine” or “who is sitting on this”.

Submit-to-filter, for the fourth time

Two selects and a Search button in a card above the list. The same pattern as machines, work requests, reports and parts — replaced everywhere with chips that apply on tap.

5

Raw date_in, and “—” when absent

The date column prints the ISO string straight from the column. What a workshop needs is how long it has been standing — “12 days ago” is the number that starts a conversation.

6

No total, no grouping, no ordering by urgency

Sorted by created_at desc with every job at equal weight, and no sum of what is open. A machine standing broken sat below a routine service booked yesterday.

7

The machine photo, unused again

Both the mobile cards and the desktop table show the machine as a text name, falling back to a literal “—” when the join misses.

8

“Job cards” is not a farm word

A workshop term used as a top-level nav item for owners and drivers too. The section is now Work; the individual record is still a job card, which is right on the record itself.

Backend untouched

Same job_cards query with the same soft-delete filter and the same status / machine search params — the chips write those params. Same six STATUSES and the same createJobCard action; the start-a-job sheet posts the same fields, with type chosen rather than hardcoded. Assignee and contractor come from columns the job-card detail page already reads. Totals still come from the DB trigger.

1

The header error is two unrelated strings

{t("machines.err.name_required")} — {t("machines.previewTitle")} renders “Name is required — Preview” when the CSV headers don’t match. It names the wrong problem, then says a heading. This is the only feedback on the most likely failure.

2

No column mapping — your sheet must match ours exactly

Headers are validated against a fixed set, so a real farm spreadsheet with Afrikaans headings, or columns in a different order, fails wholesale. Every farm already has a machine list; making them retype it into our template is why import doesn’t get used.

3

Broken rows can’t be fixed, only re-uploaded

The preview marks a row invalid and stops. To correct one typo you edit the spreadsheet in another program and start again. Rows are now editable in place.

4

Errors as stacked badges of translated codes

Each row’s Result cell renders one badge per machines.err.* key. Three problems means three red pills in a table cell, none saying what to do. Now one sentence per row, with the fix beside it.

5

Every row shown, valid or not

A 200-row sheet renders 200 preview rows, and the three that need attention are somewhere in the middle. The problems now come first; the rest is one line and a link.

6

A disabled button as the row-limit message

Over the cap, the submit greys out with a line of red text below it. A farm with 300 machines is told “too many rows” and left there — no offer to split the file or load the first batch.

7

The file picker is a dashed label with a hidden input

A <label> wrapping an sr-only input — no drag-and-drop, and it reads as a placeholder rather than a button.

8

No sense of where you are

Cards appear and disappear as state changes, with no step indicator and no way back to the file you chose. Now three visible steps.

Backend untouched

Same validateCsv rules and the same machines.err.* error keys — they are rendered as sentences instead of badge codes. Same importMachines action receiving the same raw CSV string, same MAX_IMPORT_ROWS cap, same templateCsv() download. Column mapping happens in the browser before the CSV is posted, so the server still receives a sheet in the canonical column order.
S21

Service template library — Rapid Rise staff

replaces /admin/templates

Service schedules are typed as pipe-delimited text. Every line of every template is entered into a <Textarea rows={4}> in the format Task | hours | months, and read back out by re-serialising the JSON with linesToText(). One stray pipe silently changes a maintenance interval that ships to every farm on the platform.

The audit · what was wrong
1

Service schedules typed as pipe-delimited text

Engine oil + filter | 250 | 12, four rows visible in a textarea, parsed on submit and re-serialised by linesToText() for editing. A stray pipe or a missing number silently changes an interval — for every farm using the template.

2

No blast radius shown

These are global templates. Editing one changes when machines fall due across the whole platform, and nothing on the page said how many farms or machines were affected. Now stated above the rows, before you touch anything.

3

“Delete template” — plain text, no confirm

A text-sm text-status-overdue button, one click, removing a schedule that hundreds of machines may depend on.

4

The whole editor hidden in “Edit (6 lines)”

A <details> summary is the only way to see what a template actually contains — the list shows a name and a type badge, nothing else.

5

The format is explained once, in a paragraph

“One line per row: Task | hours | months (leave a number blank if not used)” sits under the page title. Scroll past it and every textarea is unlabelled.

6

No usage data on a curation screen

Rapid Rise curates this library, and the page cannot tell staff which templates farms actually apply and which are dead weight. Usage now sits on every row.

7

A create form permanently above the list

The same fault as the admin farms page — an always-open “New template” card pushing the library down on every visit.

8

Farmer chrome on a staff tool

Same green shell as the customer app, with no marker that edits here reach every farm. It now carries the dark STAFF ONLY chrome from the admin console.

Backend untouched

Same requireRole(["rr_admin"]) gate and the same global-only query (farm_id is null). Same createTemplate / updateTemplate / deleteTemplate actions and the same lines JSON shape — the row editor serialises to the identical pipe string the textarea produced, so the server parser is unchanged. MACHINE_TYPES and TYPE_LABELS are as they were, including the “Any type” null case. Usage counts are a read against service_plans.
S22

Writing the questions for a daily check

replaces /checklists/new · /checklists/[id]/edit

You build the form blind. The builder is a stack of grey boxes, each holding a field-type dropdown, a label box, a required checkbox and a help-text box — and nowhere does it show what the driver will actually see. The person writing the questions is a manager; the person answering them is a driver holding a phone in the dark at 5am. Those two views are never shown together.

This check takes a driver about 90 seconds. Over six questions that is the most people will do every morning without skipping it.

The audit · what was wrong
1

No preview of what the driver will see

A manager writes questions in a stack of grey boxes and never sees the phone screen a driver answers on. Everything about whether a check gets done — reading level, question order, how many there are — is invisible while you build it.

2

Reordering by “Move up” / “Move down”

Two text-xs px-2 py-1 buttons per field — roughly 24px tall — that disable at the ends. Moving question eight to the top is seven round-trips. Now drag, with the buttons kept as a keyboard path.

3

“Remove field” deletes instantly, in red text

A text-xs text-status-overdue button with no confirm and no undo, sitting in the same row as the two move buttons — the smallest target on the card is the destructive one.

4

Every field shows every control at once

Type select, label box, required checkbox, help-text box and a rating-max spinner — four to five controls per question, all expanded, for a form that often has ten questions. Fifty controls on one screen. Now a one-line summary per question, expanded only when you edit it.

5

Validation only fires on save

Press Save with one unlabelled field among twelve and you get a single line — “every field needs a label” — at the bottom of the page, with no indication which one. Errors now attach to the question.

6

Field types named after data types

“Checkbox”, “Rating”, “Section break”, “Number” — the vocabulary of a form builder, not of a person deciding what to ask a driver. Renamed to what they do: yes/no, a number, pick one, a heading.

7

Labels typed straight onto inputs

The name and description fields wrap a raw <input> inside a <label> with the shared inputCls string rather than the design system’s Field and Input — so this screen drifts from every other form in the product.

8

No sense of how long the check will take

Nothing stops a manager writing twenty questions, which guarantees the check gets skipped or filled in from the bakkie. An estimate now sits under the preview.

Backend untouched

Same saveChecklistTemplate action and the same TemplatePayload shape — field_type, label, required, help_text and the rating config.max, in order. Same CHECKLIST_FIELD_TYPES values (only their labels change), same section_break handling that nulls required and help text, same requireRole(["owner","manager","mechanic","rr_admin"]) gate and global-vs-farm rule. The preview renders the same payload the driver screen consumes, so it cannot drift from what gets saved.
